title: Swampman
summary:
Donald Davidson imagined himself standing near a dead tree in a swamp when lightning strikes. His body is reduced to its elements, while by sheer coincidence (and out of different molecules) the tree is turned into his exact physical replica. The Swampman walks out of the swamp, seems to recognise Davidson's friends and return their greetings, moves into his house, and seems to write articles on radical interpretation. No one can tell the difference.

But Davidson (1987) said there is a difference. Swampman can't recognise his friends, since he never met them in the first place; and his words can't mean what Davidson's meant, because what our words and thoughts are about depends on our history of contact with the world, not only on what is in our heads. The case became a test for such "externalist" views, especially teleosemantics (Ruth Millikan, David Papineau), which says a thought's content depends on the history that shaped it. Many people find it hard to believe that Swampman has no thoughts at all; others accept that conclusion.
citations: Donald Davidson, "Knowing One's Own Mind," Proceedings and Addresses of the American Philosophical Association 60(3) (1987): 441–458
Ruth Garrett Millikan, "On Swampkinds," Mind & Language 11(1) (1996): 103–117
Karen Neander and Peter Schulte, "Teleological Theories of Mental Content," Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/content-teleological/
